exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface of Revolution: Rotation About the x-Axis

question.text:
\[ \mathbf r(x, \theta) = \big\langle x, \: e^{-x} \cos\theta, \: \textrm{_______} \big \rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(x,\theta)$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=e^{-x}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in [0,3].$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{r}?$
question.explanation:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in[a,b] $ has the position vector

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad x\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). \end{align*}

First, notice that $y=f(x) =e^{-x} \gt 0$ for all $x \in [0,3].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \big\langle x, \: e^{-x} \cos\theta, \: {\color{blue}{e^{-x} \sin\theta}} \big\rangle, \quad x \in [0,3], \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi). \]

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf r$ is ${\color{blue}{e^{-x} \sin\theta}}.$

question.text: The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(x,\theta)$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in \left[\dfrac{1}{2},1\right].$ Which of the following could be $\mathbf{r}?$
question.explanation:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in[a,b] $ has the position vector

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad x\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). \end{align*}

First, notice that $y=f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} \geq 0$ for all $x \in \left[\dfrac{1}{2},1\right].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is \[ \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \left\langle x, \: \dfrac{\cos\theta}{x}, \: \dfrac{\sin\theta}{x} \right\rangle, \quad x \in \left[\dfrac{1}{2},1\right], \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi). \]

question.text:
\[ \mathbf r(z, \theta) =\big\langle e^{1-z^2} \sin\theta,\: \textrm{__________}, \: z \big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(z,\theta)$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=e^{1-z^2}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [0,1].$ What is the second component of $\mathbf r?$
question.explanation:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(z)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(z) \sin\theta,\: f(z) \cos\theta, \: z \big\rangle, \quad z\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). \end{align*}

First, notice that $y=f(z)=e^{1-z^2} \geq 0$ for all $z \in [0,1].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\[ \mathbf{r}(z,\theta) = \big\langle e^{1-z^2} \sin\theta,\: {\color{blue}e^{1-z^2} \cos\theta}, \: z \big\rangle, \quad z \in [0,1], \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi). \]

Therefore, the second component of $\mathbf{r}$ is ${\color{blue}e^{1-z^2} \cos\theta}.$

question.text:
\[ \mathbf r(z, \theta) =\big\langle \textrm{__________},\: \sqrt{z-1} \cos\theta, \: z \big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(z,\theta)$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{z-1}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [1,10].$ What is the first component of $\mathbf r?$
question.explanation:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(z)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(z) \sin\theta,\: f(z) \cos\theta, \: z \big\rangle, \quad z\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). \end{align*}

First, notice that $y=f(z)=\sqrt{z-1} \geq 0$ for all $z \in [1,10].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\[ \mathbf{r}(z,\theta) = \big\langle{\color{blue}\sqrt{z-1} \sin\theta},\: \sqrt{z-1} \cos\theta, \: z \big\rangle, \quad z \in [1,10], \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi). \]

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{r}$ is ${\color{blue}\sqrt{z-1}\sin\theta}.$

exampleAnswers.title: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \: \text{_______} \,, \:-(x-2)^2\cos {\theta} \,, \: -(x-2)^2\sin {\theta} \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=(x-2)^2$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in [0,2]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?
question.explanation:
Notice that $y=(x-2)^2 \geq 0$ for all $x \in [0,2].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta\big\rangle, \qquad (x,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(x)=(x-2)^2,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle 1, \: f' \cos\theta, \: f' \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle 0, \: -f \sin\theta, \: f \cos\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \cos\theta \\ 0 & -f \sin\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle ff'\cos^2\theta+ff'\sin^2\theta, \: -f \cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle ff', \: -f \cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=(x-2)^2,$ we obtain $f' = 2(x-2).$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \left\langle {\color{blue}2(x-2)^3}, \: -(x-2)^2 \cos {\theta}, \: -(x-2)^2 \sin {\theta}\right\rangle. \end{align*}

example.title: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \:( 2^z-1)\sin{\theta} \,, \: (2^z-1) \cos {\theta} \,, \: \text{_______} \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=2^z-1$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [0,2]$ is given above. What is the $3$rd component of the product?
question.explanation:
Notice that $y=2^z-1 \geq 0$ for all $z \in [0,2].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(z) \sin\theta, f(z) \cos\theta, \: z\big\rangle, \qquad (z,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(z)=2^z-1,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (z,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq z \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f' \sin\theta, \: f' \cos\theta, \: 1 \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f \cos\theta, \: -f \sin\theta, \: 0 \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ f' \sin\theta & f' \cos\theta & 1\\ f \cos\theta & -f \sin\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & 1 \\ -f \sin\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix}, \:- \begin{vmatrix} f' \sin\theta & 1 \\ f \cos\theta &0\end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} f' \sin\theta & f'\cos{\theta} \\ f \cos\theta & - f\sin\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f\sin\theta, \: f\cos\theta, \: -f'f \sin^2\theta- f'f \cos^2\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f\sin\theta , \: f\cos{\theta} , \: -f'f \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=2^z-1,$ we obtain $f' =2^z\ln2 .$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \left\langle (2^z-1)\sin{\theta}, \: (2^z-1)\cos {\theta}, \: {\color{blue}-2^z\ln2(2^z-1)}\right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $x=1+y^2$ is rotated by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis for $y \in [-1,1].$
question.explanation:
Notice that $x=1+y^2 \geq 0$ for all $y \in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(y) \cos\theta, \: y, \: f(y) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \qquad (y,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(y)=1+y^2,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (y,\theta) \: : \: -1 \leq y \leq 1 , \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial y} \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f' \cos\theta, \: 1, \: f' \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle -f \sin\theta, \: 0, \: f \cos\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ f' \cos\theta & 1 & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & 0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & 1 \\ -f \sin\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f \cos\theta, \: -ff'\cos^2\theta-ff'\sin^2\theta, \: f\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f \cos\theta, \: -ff', \: f\sin\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

and

\begin{align*} \left\| \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\| &= \sqrt{\big( f \cos\theta \big)^2 + \big( -ff' \big)^2 + \big( f\sin\theta \big)^2 } \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{f^2 \big( \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta \big) + f^2(f')^2 } \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{f^2 + f^2(f')^2 } \\[3pt] &= f \sqrt{1 + (f')^2 }. \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface area is

\begin{align*} A &= \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left\| \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\| \text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D f \sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \: \text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \int_{0}^{2\pi} \!\text{d}\theta \: \text{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \cdot \theta \, \Big|_{0}^{2\pi} \: \text{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \: \text{d}y. \end{align*}

Since $f=1+y^2,$ we obtain $f' = 2y.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

\begin{align*} 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \: \text{d}y &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} (1+y^2)\sqrt{1 + \big(2y\big)^2 } \: \text{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} (1+y^2)\sqrt{1 + 4y^2 } \: \text{d}y. \end{align*}

question.text: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y=\ln z$ is rotated by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [1, e].$
question.explanation:
Notice that $y=\ln z \geq 0$ for all $z \in [1, e].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(z) \cos\theta, \: f(z) \sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle, \qquad (z,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(z)=\ln z,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (z,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq z \leq e , \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f' \cos\theta, \: f' \sin\theta, \: 1 \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle -f \sin\theta, \: f(y) \cos\theta, \: 0 \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta & 1\\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \sin\theta & 1 \\ f \cos\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix}, \:- \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & 1 \\ - f \sin\theta &0\end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle- f\cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta, \: f'f \cos^2\theta+f'f \sin^2\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle -f\cos\theta , \: -f\sin{\theta} , \: f'f \big\rangle. \end{align*}

and

\begin{align*} \left\| \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\| &= \sqrt{\big( -f\cos\theta \big)^2 + \big( -f\sin{\theta} \big)^2 + \big( f'f \big)^2 } \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{f^2 \big( \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta \big) + f^2(f')^2 } \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{f^2 + f^2(f')^2 } \\[3pt] &= f \sqrt{1 + (f')^2 }. \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface area is

\begin{align*} A &= \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left\| \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\| \text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D f \sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \: \text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{e} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \int_{0}^{2\pi} \!\text{d}\theta \: \text{d}z \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{e} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \cdot \theta \, \Big|_{0}^{2\pi} \: \text{d}z \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{e} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \: \text{d}z. \end{align*}

Since $f=\ln z,$ we obtain $f' = \dfrac 1z.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

\begin{align*} 2\pi \int_{1}^{e} f\sqrt{1 + (f')^2 } \: \text{d}z &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{e} \ln z\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac 1z\right)^2 } \: \text{d}z \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{e} \ln z\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{z^2} } \: \text{d}z. \end{align*}
